Tea first reached Europe around 1610, when ships of the Dutch East India Company brought it to the Netherlands from Japan and China. Portuguese travellers had written about it earlier, but the Dutch made it a trade.

At first tea was a costly medicine and a luxury. It reached London in the 1650s, and Catherine of Braganza, the Portuguese wife of Charles II, made it fashionable at court. The English East India Company then built a huge trade in it from Canton. Drinking it with sugar, grown by enslaved Africans in the Caribbean, tied the habit to the Atlantic slave trade.

By the 1800s tea was Britain's everyday drink. Britain paid China for it in silver, then sold Indian opium to get the silver back, which led to the First Opium War. The British then began growing tea in India after the Assam tea plant was found in 1823. In China, tea drinking was already old: see The Classic of Tea, written around 760.
